title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: Past 0.68 price weeks show 1.2% below baseline (vs 0.67); noise-adjusted, consistent across 12 weeks.

drivers.name: competitor store opening across street
drivers.evidence: One past similar event: 5-10% sales drop observed; noise-adjusted estimate shrunk to 5%.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 438.2. Price increased 1.5% to $0.68, which historically correlates with a 1.2% sales drop (noise-adjusted). Competitor entry across the street is a known demand threat; past similar events show 8-10% lift in competitor traffic, with 5% average demand loss for affected stores. Evidence is moderate (one past event, store-level impact). Combined effect shrinks toward 1.0 due to thin data. No promotion or holiday. Classical model is blind to new competition and price sensitivity. Adjust down conservatively.

brief:
PRODUCT: Bananas (per lb) | category Produce | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08 (4 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.7 - 555.9 | 10%-90%: 346.6 - 529.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
